rows.verified: Occupational asthma is an allergic reaction that can occur after workplace exposure to respiratory sensitisers such as flour or wood dust.
Respiratory sensitisation can create a hypersensitive state in the airways.
After sensitisation, further exposure to relatively low concentrations may trigger an asthma attack.
Work-related asthma also includes pre-existing asthma made worse by workplace airway irritants.
Rosin-based solder flux fume is identified by HSE as a leading occupational-asthma cause in electronics and assembly work.
HSE evidence shows that reducing flour dust at source can materially reduce baker-asthma exposure.
Dutyholders should identify respiratory sensitisers and manage exposure through risk assessment and effective controls.
Regular health surveillance is required where workers remain exposed to recognised respiratory sensitisers such as rosin solder flux fume.
Occupational-asthma risk depends on the sensitiser, airborne concentration, task duration, ventilation, control reliability and individual susceptibility.
Occupational-asthma guidance is exposure- and person-specific and is not an exact parcel-level illness probability.
Metalworking fluids are neat oils or water-based fluids used to lubricate and cool metal machining and shaping operations.
Exposure to metalworking fluids can cause skin irritation or dermatitis.
Metalworking-fluid exposure can contribute to occupational asthma, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, bronchitis and other breathing problems.
Exposure routes include inhaling machining mist, direct skin contact, entry through damaged skin and ingestion caused by poor hygiene.
COSHH requires exposure by inhalation, ingestion or skin contact to be prevented where reasonably practicable or otherwise adequately controlled.
Dutyholders should maintain fluid quality and monitor bacterial contamination in water-mix fluids.
Engineering controls such as enclosure and extraction are used to reduce airborne metalworking-fluid mist during CNC machining.
Where exposure remains, health surveillance and prompt occupational-health referral are part of the control programme.
Metalworking-fluid risk depends on fluid chemistry, machine enclosure, mist generation, microbial condition, skin contact, maintenance and hygiene.
Metalworking-fluid evidence is process-, machine-, fluid- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level respiratory or skin-disease probability.
